description: We are NIVORA, an ambitious and creative team of Software Engineering students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our team is driven by curiosity, innovation, and a shared passion for technology. We believe that great ideas can come from anyone, and that combining different skills and perspectives is the key to developing meaningful solutions.
summary:
NIVORA is an interactive 3D Mars mission trainer designed for children ages 7–12. Instead of only teaching space science through facts, NIVORA lets young players experience the engineering trade-offs of running a Martian outpost.

Across five mission rounds, players manage life support, food and water, power, rover exploration, and radiation safety. Every major decision has a benefit and a cost: producing more oxygen uses more energy, collecting more science can reduce safety margins, and exploring farther consumes more rover battery.

NIVORA connects these decisions to real NASA science using historical Mars radiation measurements from NASA RadLab, space-weather context from DONKI, NASA life-support reference values, and Mars Trek terrain data. NASA reference values are clearly separated from NIVORA’s educational simulation values.

The result is a browser-based, bilingual English/Arabic mission experience that teaches systems thinking through consequences, replayability, and real scientific context.
details:
What it does and how it works

NIVORA is a bilingual English/Arabic, offline-capable Progressive Web App that puts children ages 7–12 in command of an interactive 3D Mars habitat.

Instead of quizzing space facts, NIVORA asks the player to make engineering decisions under limited resources. Across five mission rounds, the child balances oxygen, water, food, power, rover exploration, science, and radiation safety. Each round presents two or three decision options, creating 48 possible decision paths across a complete mission.

The player explores a custom WebGL Mars habitat with interactive areas including the greenhouse, oxygen lab, water recycler, solar array, habitat, rover bay, fabrication lab, and storm shelter.

Each round introduces a different engineering tension. For example, the player can boost oxygen production for +10 oxygen at a cost of −7 energy, or conserve power and receive a smaller +4 oxygen gain for −3 energy. Other rounds ask the player to grow more food or conserve water, prioritize life support, science, or rover operations from one shared power reserve, choose a safer rover route or a higher-science route, and decide whether to shelter immediately or briefly finish an experiment.

After each choice, mission resources change visibly and ECHO/5 explains the consequence. At the end of the mission, the player receives one of five Mission Styles — Safety-First Commander, Science Explorer, Resource Strategist, Mars Pathfinder, or Balanced Mission Commander — encouraging another playthrough with a different strategy.

Benefits and intended impact

Most space education explains outcomes: a rover landed, a plant grew, or an experiment succeeded. NIVORA focuses on the decision-making behind those outcomes.

Its goal is to teach systems thinking: when oxygen, energy, water, science, exploration, and crew safety compete for limited resources, improving one system may create a cost somewhere else.

Replayability comes from 48 possible decision paths and 27 Mission DNA configurations. Different choices produce different resource stories and leadership profiles, helping children understand that engineering problems rarely have one cost-free answer.

NIVORA can operate offline after its required assets are cached, supports desktop and mobile layouts, and includes English and Arabic with full right-to-left support, making it suitable for classrooms and homes in a wider range of connectivity and language environments.

Real NASA science, honestly used

NIVORA integrates four NASA resources as scientific context while keeping NASA measurements separate from educational simulation values.

NASA RadLab provides historical Mars-surface radiation measurements from MSL-RAD/Curiosity, including a verified value of 4.6009493 µGy/hour.

NASA DONKI provides historical space-weather context through a documented 2024-05-11 event chain that includes an X5.8 solar flare and a CME with a reported speed of 1263 km/s.

NASA's Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document provides crew-day reference values such as 0.895 kg of oxygen and 3.217 kg of potable water.

NASA Mars Trek provides Jezero Crater context through CTX imagery and a MOLA elevation profile containing 100 points across 228.309 km.

These NASA values are presented as scientific references. NIVORA's resource gains, losses, thresholds, and scores are clearly identified as educational simulation values. The game does not convert NASA measurements into gameplay points or infer Mars radiation dose from DONKI events.

Tools, languages, and software

NIVORA was developed with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript. Its 3D environment uses a custom WebGL/WebGL2 renderer and procedural geometry rather than a commercial game engine.

The project also uses JSON-based scientific data, browser LocalStorage for progress, the Web Speech API for optional narration, and Progressive Web App technologies including a web manifest and service worker for offline use.

Automated browser testing with Playwright was used to verify gameplay behavior, NASA-data handling, accessibility, Arabic/RTL support, mobile layouts, and offline behavior.

No special hardware, account, backend database, or installation is required to play the final web version.

How it is creative

NIVORA combines real NASA scientific context with a visible decision-cost mechanic.

Instead of using NASA data as decoration, the data helps explain why mission systems matter. The child then experiences the simulated consequence of a choice while seeing a clear boundary between authentic scientific measurements and educational game values.

Mission DNA adds another layer of systems thinking. The child creates an IF–THEN automation rule that can later activate automatically during a simulated mission emergency. This introduces conditional logic, automation, and unintended side effects in a form that young players can experience rather than only read about.

The Mission Style system then transforms the player's decisions into a reflection of how they approached safety, science, efficiency, and exploration.

Factors the team considered

We prioritized scientific honesty, age-appropriate language, accessibility, bilingual English/Arabic support, right-to-left layout, mobile usability, offline resilience, and replayability without unnecessary interface complexity.

We also deliberately kept the project's scope honest: NIVORA uses stylized procedural 3D rather than claiming photorealistic reconstruction, NASA values remain scientific references rather than game scores, and all safety thresholds and mission consequences are presented as educational simulation rather than operational NASA guidance.
